query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting part of a CoCrFeNi refractory HEA with manganese (to form CoCrFeMnNi) will enhance its irradiation-induced dislocation density and promote a stable compressive stress state, which together improve its mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and hardness) under high-temperature and irradiation conditions without compromising its phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi refractory high-entropy alloy with a near-equiatomic composition and stable FCC solid-solution phase.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding manganese to transform CoCrFeNi into CoCrFeMnNi.
generation.conditions: Irradiation by sequential heavy (Kr) and light (He) ions at reactor-relevant fluences and high temperatures, where the formation of irradiation-induced defects is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion due to Mn addition promotes the formation of numerous fine dislocation clusters and limits the growth of helium bubbles.
generation.mechanism: The manganese substitution increases lattice distortion, which lowers defect mobility and encourages the formation of a high density of small radiation-induced dislocation loops and helium bubbles. This results in increased compressive macrostresses and improved resistance to irradiation-induced degradation, while preserving solid-solution phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the base CoCrFeNi alloy, the Mn-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy will exhibit higher hardness and yield strength under irradiation and high-temperature conditions, with maintained phase and compositional stability.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi HEA without manganese addition, which under similar irradiation conditions shows lower dislocation density and less pronounced compressive stresses.
generation.boundary: The improved performance is expected under sequential Kr and He irradiation at high temperatures; deviations in irradiation energy, fluence, or temperature beyond reactor-relevant conditions may alter the defect behavior and mechanical responses.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., strength and hardness increments) is uncertain and may depend on the optimal Mn concentration and specific irradiation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with the CoCrFeNi composition and one with the modified CoCrFeMnNi composition. Subject both sets to sequential ion irradiation using krypton and helium at reactor-relevant energies and fluences while maintaining high temperature. Post-irradiation, perform microstructural characterization using TEM and XRD, and assess mechanical properties with nanoindentation and hardness testing.
measurements: Macroscopic stress state using XRD measurements
Hardness and yield strength through nanoindentation and mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy either exhibits no significant increase in irradiation-induced dislocation density/compressive stresses or shows degradation in phase stability/mechanical performance compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy under the same irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Composition and Structure of Initial CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
cited_evidence.text: The elemental content and main phases of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were preserved despite successive irradiation with krypton (280 keV, 5 × 1015 cm−2) and helium (40 keV, 2 × 1017 cm−2) ions; new phases did not emerge, but several blisters formed on the surface of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, although with a smaller average size than in Ni. Fewer large blisters formed in the HEA probably because of lattice distortion, low defect mobility and weakened helium bubble formation [,]. It can be seen that Kr irradiation enhances the surface damage leading to blister formation at room temperature compared to He-only irradiation, which was carried out in []. Analysis of the results of the study of macrostresses and density of dislocations in HEAs showed that the main changes obtained as a result of sample irradiation are probably associated with the formation, interaction and migration of radiation-induced defects and their clusters, which modified stresses in the alloys. The compressive stresses in HEAs after irradiation could be caused by the creation of many small point defects, defect clusters [] and helium bubbles [], which are constrained by the HEA lattice, while in pure Ni, larger defect

Sequential irradiation with Kr and He ions led to a change from tensile to compressive stresses in the HEAs in both Regions I and II compared to unirradiated states. But in Region I, stress in Ni remained tensile, while compressive stresses of −54 MPa and −258 MPa formed in CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. In Region II, compressive macrostresses reached larger values of −131.5 MPa, −300 MPa and −613.5 MPa in Ni, CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. The trend of compressive stress formation similar to He-only irradiation could be due to increased damage and helium bubbles accumulation in the HEAs. Irradiation by Kr ions led to a decrease in the dislocation density by 1.6–2.3 times in Regions I and II and sequential irradiation with Kr and He ions to an increase of dislocation densities in Region II by 11–15 times for CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. Most notable macrostress and dislocation density changes were observed in the peak helium implantation region. After irradiation, the CoCrFeMnNi HEA was characterized by higher macrostresses and dislocation density compared to CoCrFeNi.
